title: The Receiving Authority
passages:
Fenn's rig didn't announce itself. No horn, no hail on the open channel — just the crunch of tires on the chalk line and the diesel cough settling into idle. The pump hall's big doors stood open on the grade, Saul's pencil frozen mid-tally on the clipboard, six scrubber cases already strapped to the pallet jack and the other five waiting their turn. Brill stood with her arms folded, lamp light catching the grease on her jaw, watching the rig's cab door swing down.

Fenn stepped out in the same coat they'd worn at Anza, badge catching the first light. No sidearm visible, no backup visible. Just the serve order folded in their gloved hand and the look of someone who'd already decided how the morning went.

"Didn't think you'd make the grade before eight," Kass said from the pallet jack. Their voice carried flat across the concrete, no surprise, no welcome.

Fenn didn't look at them. Eyes tracked the stacked cases, the dies on the workbench — Voss's square brass and the chipped crescent Ospina had brought down — then settled on the back room door where Voss had disappeared twenty minutes ago. "Desk's terms didn't change. Produce the forger or surrender the witness. First light was the deadline."

"First light's here," Ospina said. They stood by the reader cradle, live ring still hot from the crimp against Voss's die. The counter on their flagged authority blinked red in the reader's display, a wound that wouldn't close. "We've got eleven cases matched to two dies. The resealer's in the back. The witness is on the set."

"Freight is not a record." Fenn unfolded the serve order, the paper stiff with cold. "Red score is Anza sheltering a contested man. Eleven cases clean or dirty doesn't move the board. You put a forger on the plate or you put Marlowe in my rig. My clearance turns at eight. When it does, the reclamation unit rolls and I write this hall off the line."

Fenn tapped the wall reader's clock display with one gloved finger. The green numbers burned 07:56. "Four minutes. Starting now."

"Standing offer holds," Fenn added, voice dropping to the register that closed deals. "Full compressor power for the brother the hour the sister signs the witness over. That's the only trade the desk recognizes."

Rhea's name wasn't in this room. She was back at Anza relay shop, hand-pumping Ivo's respirator, two cartridges left. But the weight of it landed on Kass's shoulders anyway, visible in the way their jaw tightened.

Kass’s jaw stayed tight. They didn’t look at Fenn. They looked at Brill.

Brill didn’t unfold her arms. “I don’t move scrubbers for a ghost. You want cases out of this hall, you put a living name behind badge 2244. That’s the rule I learned at Culvert Nine, and I haven’t unlearned it because Anza turned red.”

Kass glanced at Miko. Miko was still in her coat, the overlap log heavy in her pocket. She hadn’t spoken since she loaded the pallet jack.

“Miko,” Kass said.

Miko pulled the log from her pocket and set it on the workbench between Voss’s stamp and the chipped crescent. The pages were grease-stained and the ink smelled of cold shop oil. She flipped to the twenty-first shift change and slid the book across the concrete.

“Overflow ring,” Miko said. “That’s when one shift borrows a seal from the next because their own run came up short. The ring was drawn here, at this station, under a signature that looks like a name.” Miko tapped the page. “But it’s a credential with no living hand behind it. Badge 2244 exists on paper. The person it belonged to doesn’t clock in anywhere. It’s a mark that leads nowhere.”

Fenn checked their watch. 07:58. “So your ghost counter signed for ballast and then walked off the roster. That doesn’t clean a chain. That makes it dirtier.”

“It means you can’t catch him by the book tonight,” Kass said. “The taped-glove man isn’t on any plate we can reach. If we wait for a name behind 2244, Brill doesn’t move a case, the scrubbers stay in Culvert Nine, and Ivo’s respirator dies on Rhea’s cart.”

Brill’s lip curled. “Then tell your loader to find a living name, or I keep my stockpile.”

“We don’t need his name,” Kass said. “We need a chain that reads clean. If the receiving side has a living authority, the sender side can stay orphaned. The book won’t flag a chain just because one strike was made by a dead credential.”

“You’re saying you’ll launder a reseal with a blank on the sender jaw,” Fenn said. Their voice was flat. “My desk doesn’t accept orphaned strikes.”

“Not launder,” Kass said. “Close. We clean it without naming the man who counted Marlowe under the lid. That keeps your file red on one count, but it puts eleven seals back on the board before eight. Unless you’d rather serve the watch and write off Anza entirely.”

Fenn’s eyes flicked to the wall clock. 07:59. One minute.

“One minute,” Fenn said. “When my clearance turns, I make the call. If this hall doesn’t have a clean chain on the board, the reclamation unit rolls and I take Marlowe whether he’s listed or not.”

They turned and walked back to their rig, boots crunching on chalk. The engine idled, waiting.

Miko left the log open on the bench. The signature stared up at them, a name with no body behind it.

Ospina lifted their hand off the cradle and the red counter kept blinking on the little display, patient as a wound that wouldn't scab. "Say it out loud," they told Kass. "The whole room should hear who eats tonight and who doesn't."

Kass pushed off the pallet jack. "A reseal chain closes on three points." They held up greasy fingers. "The sender strike, where a case gets sealed back up. The receiving counter, a living man who takes the goods in and says he saw what's under the seal. And the reader cradle, where a seal authority sets the ferrule — the little collar that locks a seal so nobody pops it without cutting a fresh strike." They tipped their head at Ospina's blinking display. "The cradle's got a live ring in it. That part's not the trouble."

"Then what is," Brill said, arms still folded.

"The counter." Kass looked at Ospina. "It won't read a ring. It won't read a flag. It reads a name on Anza's plate — a living man on the crew roll, breathing, who can put his hand on these eleven cases and tell you what's inside."

"Which can't be mine," Ospina said. "My authority's live, but it's flagged for review at Kettering's morning desk. A flagged ring can set a ferrule. It can't stand up and be the man who watched the goods go by. The counter reads a name, not a badge with a hole in it."

Brill unfolded one arm. Just one. "You've got a name on your plate. The ballast you dragged in. Your own ring countersigned him onto the crew roll."

"Marlowe," Ospina said, quiet.

"There's your living witness," Brill said. "He was inside the box. He watched the seals go on from the wrong side of the lid. He can name every case in this stack better than any manifest you'll ever pull." She refolded the arm. "Put him on the receiving jaw and I move your scrubbers."

The hall went still except the reader's red blink. Kass didn't look pleased. Neither did Ospina.

"You're both stepping around it," Ospina said. "So I'll step on it. Sign Marlowe as receiving authority and it isn't free. There's a claim riding that man — the taped-glove counter, badge 2244, the hands claim, still live. A living man who signs as authority becomes cargo with a name attached. And a live claim can still take cargo with a name. We'd list him to feed the node and hand whoever holds 2244 the right to walk him out the door."

"Buy the winter with the man," Kass said. "Same trade Fenn's been waving since Anza. Just in a cleaner coat."

"So find a different living name," Brill said.

"There isn't one." Kass spread their hands. "Not on any plate I can reach before Fenn's clock turns over. Marlowe's the only living man who was under that lid and can stand behind what he saw. It's him or the node freezes."

Nobody had an answer to that. On the wall reader the clock burned 07:59 and just sat there, refusing to move.

Kass crossed the concrete to the set on the workbench — the little bulb-lit screen holding the open channel back to Anza relay shop, where a man was supposed to be laid out on Teodoro's couch with his shoulder splinted and his memory coming back to him in pieces.

They meant to ask if he was awake.

He was already breathing on the line. Slow, even, close to the pickup — the breathing of a man who'd been listening the whole time.

Fenn had a hand on the cab step when the set caught them — that slow, even breathing on the open channel, a man listening who had no business listening. They took the hand off the step and came back across the chalk.

"No." The serve order came unfolded again, held up like it settled the room. "A man under a serve order can't be a clean authority. That's not me being difficult, that's the desk. Marlowe's contested — live claim riding him, 2244, my order on his bunk. You put a contested man on the receiving jaw and the reader knows it. Board reads sheltering. Reads exactly what's had Anza red since yesterday. That's the whole reason my file won't close."

"Then don't serve him," Ospina said.

"I'm not serving him. I'm telling you he doesn't qualify."

"He qualifies." Ospina never raised their voice. "Your desk wrote the rule. A living man on the crew roll, countersigned by a live seal, is a valid receiving witness. It's in the book you carry." They nodded at the folded paper in Fenn's glove. "Marlowe's on Anza's plate as living crew. I countersigned him onto it while my ring was clean — not flagged, clean. The countersign stands. He's the one living name in this hall your desk will read."

Fenn's jaw worked. "The claim—"

"Two lines, two pens," Kass said from the pallet jack. "Pell's claim voided the hour Marlowe got a name. The hands claim didn't. You'd have flagged it the same way if it were your board."

"So he's valid and he's claimed. That's not a clean witness, that's a—"

"That's a witness you can take." Ospina let it sit. "Call your unit. Serve him off that plate, haul him to Kettering. Go ahead." A beat. "And watch what it does to your morning."

Fenn stopped.

"Receiving counter reads a living name," Ospina said. "Take the name off the plate, the jaw goes empty. No living counter, no clean chain. Eleven seals stay orphaned on your board and your file's red at eight, same as it's been red all night. You don't close anything. You watch Anza freeze from a warmer rig, and you drive home with a red file and an empty bunk."

"That's not a threat," Fenn said, quiet now.

"It's a rule. Yours. We're only reading it back."

"You think I came down here to take a man." Fenn's voice thinned. "I came for a spotless record. That's what closes clean at the desk. A reclamation isn't spotless — it's red with the body removed. That's not the file I drive home."

"Then you already know," Ospina said. "The only spotless thing in this hall is standing on that man. The second your unit touches him, it isn't spotless anymore."

Fenn looked at the clock. 07:59, still, refusing to turn. They looked at the order sagging in their glove, at the eleven cases with their two dies, at the reader's red counter blinking its patient wound. The serve order didn't get them a clean file. It got them the opposite, and they'd written the reason themselves.

Nobody moved to help them out of it. Brill had unfolded both arms now, watching the way you watch a scale settle. Miko's hand rested flat on the open log, the dead credential staring up at the bulb.

Fenn's mouth opened. Nothing came.

And on the set, close to the pickup, the breathing changed — caught, held, and let go. The breath of a man who'd stopped listening and started deciding to talk.
